newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian Moslem-backed party cries poll fraud.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian Moslem-backed party cries poll fraud.

text.p: Indonesia's Moslem-backed minority party, alleging mass fraud, said on Tuesday it wanted a rerun of last week's general elections throughout the Sampang regency, not just in localised points.
Electoral officials said there would be fresh voting on Wednesday at 86 polling stations at Sampang, a devoutly Moslem coastal town on Madura island off East Java.
They said the vote would cover stations whose ballots were destroyed after the polls last Thursday by a crowd charging that the election had been rigged in favour of the ruling Golkar party.

Hasan Asy'ari, secretary of the Sampang branch of the minority United Development Party (PPP), said the party wanted a revote in all 1,033 polling stations in the Sampang regency and not just in the 86 places whose ballot boxes were destroyed at the district head office on the town's main street.
He told reporters the party had decided not to supply witnesses for the new vote, but stopped short of calling for a boycott, which would be illegal.
"We are saying that we will not join the election, but it does not mean we are boycotting the election or supporting Golput," Asy'ari said.
Golput, which literally means White Group, is the informal movement by which Indonesian voters spoil their ballots or do not vote as a form of protest against the tightly-controlled electoral system.
"Our witnesses saw irregularities and violations of election rules in all the polling stations," Asy'ari said.

The ruling Golkar party swept a record 74 percent of the votes nationwide, with the PPP winning almost 23 percent, after an election campaign that saw the worst political violence in the country in three decades.
PPP officials in Jakarta have charged that there were widespread irregularities in voting and said the party would decide on Thursday whether or not to accept the result.
The only other party legally entitled to contest the poll, the fragmented Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), saw its vote plunge to three percent from 15 percent in 1992.
It said on Tuesday it might have to withdraw from parliament for lack of enough members to satisfy house rules.

The government has deployed hundreds of extra troops in Sampang after PPP supporters destroyed a police post and damaged several shops and banks in a rampage that started on Thursday night and continued to Sunday morning.
Residents said the town was normal on Tuesday as shops opened and the main street was crowded with yellow tricycle taxis as police and soldiers kept a low profile.
Visitors to the town on Monday night were stopped and had their cars searched on the outskirts, while two armoured cars were seen patrolling the streets.
"It is like they are getting ready for a war rather than a festival of democracy," the PPP's Asy'ari said.
Asy'ari said the party organisation was not angry, but he said the people had perhaps lost control because they had seen many violations of the electoral rules over the last few elections.
"Maybe their level of political awareness has been increasing and they now know their political rights," he said.
